equation_request.abstract: Quantum walks have been very useful in developing search algorithms in quantum information, in particular for devising of spatial search algorithms. However, the construction of continuous-time quantum search algorithms in two-dimensional lattices has proved difficult, requiring additional degrees of freedom. Here, we demonstrate that continuous-time quantum walk search is possible in two-dimensions by changing the search topology to a graphene lattice, utilising the Dirac point in the energy spectrum. This is made possible by making a change to standard methods of marking a particular site in the lattice. Various ways of marking a site are shown to result in successful search protocols. We further establish that the search can be adapted to transfer probability amplitude across the lattice between specific lattice sites thus establishing a line of communication between these sites.

specification.problem: Continuous-time quantum walk spatial search on a 2D graphene (honeycomb) lattice, using the Dirac point of the spectrum, with modified site-marking so that the marked site is found without extra degrees of freedom; also adapting the search to transfer amplitude between specific lattice sites.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Theoretical Hamiltonian-evolution (analog continuous-time) search on a finite graphene lattice; not a gate-circuit algorithm. Specific marking Hamiltonians and scaling results are not given in the abstract and are reconstructed only as generic background.

equations.label: Search Hamiltonian
equations.description: Generic walk Hamiltonian on graphene lattice plus on-site marking of site w; the abstract says marking differs from standard methods, so this is a generic form only.
equations.justification: Standard continuous-time quantum walk search form; the paper's modified marking is not specified in the abstract.
assumptions: Marking by on-site potential is only one of several possible marking methods

equations.label: Time evolution
equations.description: Unitary evolution of the walker amplitude over the lattice.
equations.justification: Definition of continuous-time quantum walk dynamics.

equations.label: Success probability
equations.description: Probability of finding the walker at marked site w; for transfer, w is the receiving site with start at a specific site.
equations.justification: Natural figure of merit for search and for state transfer between sites.
assumptions: Initial state is delocalized for search or localized at a source site for transfer

registers.name: lattice
registers.size: N (number of lattice sites; log2 N qubits if embedded)
registers.role: Single-particle position register; walker occupies one site (the graphene lattice includes both sublattices)

specification.initial_state: Search: uniform superposition over all sites (or a state near the Dirac-point eigenstates), |s> = N^{-1/2} sum_x |x>. Transfer: localized state |v> at the source site.

steps.description: Build the graphene adjacency matrix A on a finite lattice with assumed periodic boundaries and choose the marked site w (or receiver site) with marking strength epsilon.
Prepare the initial state on the lattice register (uniform superposition for search, localized source site for transfer).
Evolve under the marked Hamiltonian H for time t, tuned to the time where the probability at w peaks.
Evaluate the amplitude at the target site to assess search or transfer success.

specification.measurement: Position-basis measurement of the lattice register after evolution time t; the outcome is the site w with probability p_w(t) (eq_3). Repeat over runs to estimate p_w.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Scan or choose evolution time t to maximize the estimated p_w(t); declare the most frequent outcome as the marked site (search) or check arrival at the receiver site (transfer). Repeat runs as needed for amplification.
assumptions: Finite graphene lattice with periodic boundaries assumed
Analog Hamiltonian simulation; any gate-circuit embedding is not specified
Lattice register treated as a single-particle position space; qubit encoding is not given
